question.text: Vikram, a day trader in Hyderabad, made INR 2 lakh profit in a bull market. He now trades with concentrated bets in a single sector, ignoring diversification. He says, "I have a special ability to read the market." When his trades go wrong, he blames market manipulation. This combination of biases is BEST described as:

answer.text: Loss aversion combined with anchoring bias
Mental accounting combined with framing bias
Endowment bias combined with status quo bias
Overconfidence bias combined with self-attribution bias

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook defines Overconfidence as unwarranted faith in one's own judgment, visible in portfolio concentration, sector bias and excessive trading. Self-Attribution Bias makes investors take credit for successes and blame others or external factors for failures. Vikram's sector concentration and "special ability" claim point to overconfidence; blaming "market manipulation" when trades fail is classic self-attribution. The Trap: Loss aversion would make Vikram hold losing positions to avoid realising the loss, not trade more aggressively. Mental accounting involves treating money differently by source — related, but not the primary issue here, which is overconfidence driving concentrated trading. Note: The workbook discusses overconfidence and self-attribution together because they reinforce each other — past wins are mis-attributed to skill, which then fuels even more concentrated bets.
